parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the SCANTRON answer sheet with a pencil. (The paper has no printed section headings; items 1–40 are Economics and 41–80 Accounting – shown in each question's 'section' field.)

parts.title: Part II – Work Out and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains five short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently, every calculation was verified in Python (tools/src_matric/business_economics_2018/verify_calcs.py) and answers were checked against the Eritrean MoE Business and Economics textbooks Grades 10–12. See confidence and review_flag on each question.
exam.textbook_note: No Grade 9 Business and Economics textbook was supplied. All exam content maps to Grades 10–12.

questions.stem: Economics can best be defined as

options.A: the study of how to reduce inflation and unemployment.
options.C: the study of the use of scarce resources to satisfy unlimited human wants.
options.D: the study of how a society ought to allocate its unlimited resources.
options.E: the application of sophisticated mathematical models to address social problems.

explanation_steps: Textbook: “Economics is the study of how individuals and societies choose to use their scarce resources in order to satisfy their unlimited wants.”
A is only one macro problem; B is only one branch; D wrongly calls resources unlimited; E describes a tool, not the subject. Answer: C.
tips: Every definition of economics contains the pair scarce resources ↔ unlimited wants.

similar_questions.stem: The basic economic problem arises because

options.A: wants are limited and resources are unlimited
options.B: resources are scarce relative to unlimited wants

explanation_steps: Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants. Answer: B.

questions.stem: An economic system

options.A: requires a grouping of private markets linked to one another.
options.B: refers to the way a society allocates its scarce resources and makes the three economic decisions.
options.C: requires a centralized authority to coordinate economic activity.
options.D: is a plan which allows a firm to make profit at some other firm’s expense.

explanation_steps: An economic system is the way a society organises the use of its scarce resources to answer the three basic questions: what, how and for whom to produce.
A describes only a market economy and C only a command economy. Answer: B.
tips: Traditional, command, market and mixed systems all answer the same three questions in different ways.

similar_questions.stem: The three basic economic questions are

options.A: what, how and for whom to produce
options.B: where, when and why to produce
options.C: who, when and how much to save
options.D: what to import, export and tax

explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: A firm with one or more owners and with limited liability is a
explanation_steps: Sole proprietorships and (general) partnerships have UNLIMITED liability (textbook p.17–19).
A corporation is a legal entity separate from its owners (shareholders), who are liable only up to their investment – limited liability; it can have one or many owners. Answer: D.
tips: Limited liability ↔ corporation (share company); unlimited liability ↔ sole proprietorship and partnership.

similar_questions.stem: Which form of business organisation has unlimited liability?
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: E ‘public company’ is itself a kind of corporation with limited liability; D is keyed because the textbook classifies business organisations as sole proprietorship, partnership and corporation.

questions.stem: Modern transportation systems

options.A: equalize prices by making it possible to move goods from a place where their supply exceeds their demand.

explanation_steps: Textbook benefits of transportation: price equalisation (moving goods from low-price surplus areas), employment, national and international trade, national defence and unity.
All four statements are benefits. Answer: E.
tips: When every option is a true benefit listed in the textbook, choose ‘All of the above’.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an economic benefit of good roads?
explanation_steps: Answer: D.

questions.stem: Question 5–7 are based on Figure 1 (production possibility curve). If the economy is operating at Point C, the opportunity cost of producing an additional 15 units of orange is [Figure 1 (PPC): Orange on the vertical axis, Eggs on the horizontal axis. On the curve: A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30 eggs, 35 oranges), C (50, 20), D (60, 0). Inside the curve: E (30, 20). Outside: F (40, 35).]
questions.image_alt: Figure 1. Production possibility curve: Orange (vertical axis, 0–50) against Eggs (horizontal axis, 0–70). The bowed-out curve passes through A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30, 35), C (50, 20) and D (60, 0). Point E (30, 20) lies inside the curve; point F (40, 35) lies outside it. Dashed lines mark 30, 40 and 50 eggs and 20 and 35 oranges.
explanation_steps: At C the economy produces 50 eggs and 20 oranges. 15 more oranges → 35 oranges, the unlabelled point on the curve at 30 eggs.
Eggs fall from 50 to 30: 50 − 30 = 20 eggs given up. Answer: B.
tips: Opportunity cost on a PPC = the amount of the OTHER good you must give up when moving along the curve.

similar_questions.stem: On a PPC, moving from (20 cloth, 40 food) to (35 cloth, 25 food) gives 15 more cloth. The opportunity cost is
explanation_steps: Food falls 40 → 25 = 15. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Based on Figure 1: If the economy were operating at point E, [Figure 1 (PPC): Orange on the vertical axis, Eggs on the horizontal axis. On the curve: A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30 eggs, 35 oranges), C (50, 20), D (60, 0). Inside the curve: E (30, 20). Outside: F (40, 35).]
questions.image_alt: Figure 1. Production possibility curve: Orange (vertical axis, 0–50) against Eggs (horizontal axis, 0–70). The bowed-out curve passes through A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30, 35), C (50, 20) and D (60, 0). Point E (30, 20) lies inside the curve; point F (40, 35) lies outside it. Dashed lines mark 30, 40 and 50 eggs and 20 and 35 oranges.

options.A: the opportunity cost of 20 additional units of eggs is 10 units of orange.
options.B: the opportunity cost of 20 additional units of eggs is 20 units of orange.
options.C: the opportunity cost of 20 additional units of eggs is 30 units of orange.
options.D: 20 additional units of eggs can be produced with no change on orange production.
options.E: 30 additional units of eggs can be produced with no change on orange production.

explanation_steps: E (30 eggs, 20 oranges) is INSIDE the curve – resources are unemployed.
Moving right to C (50 eggs, 20 oranges) adds 20 eggs with oranges unchanged: zero opportunity cost.
30 more eggs (to 60) would require oranges to fall to 0, so E is wrong. Answer: D.
tips: Inside the PPC, output of one good can rise without giving up any of the other.

similar_questions.stem: An economy is inside its PPC. This means
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Based on Figure 1: Point F represents a [Figure 1 (PPC): Orange on the vertical axis, Eggs on the horizontal axis. On the curve: A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30 eggs, 35 oranges), C (50, 20), D (60, 0). Inside the curve: E (30, 20). Outside: F (40, 35).]

The bowed-out curve passes through A (0 eggs, 40 oranges), an unlabelled point (30, 35), C (50, 20) and D (60, 0). Point E (30, 20) lies inside the curve; point F (40, 35) lies outside it. options.A: combination of production that can be reached if we increase the production of eggs by 20 units with the current resources available.
options.B: combination of production that is inefficient because there are unemployed resources.
options.C: combination of production that is unobtainable because there are limited resources.
options.D: combination of production that can be reached if technology becomes outdated.

explanation_steps: F (40 eggs, 35 oranges) lies OUTSIDE the curve.
Points outside the PPC cannot be produced with current resources and technology – unattainable. Only growth (more resources or better technology) could reach it. Answer: C.
tips: Outside = unattainable; on = efficient; inside = inefficient.

similar_questions.stem: A point outside a country’s PPC can be reached only if
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: The real value of money is measured in terms of
explanation_steps: The value of money is the amount of goods and services a unit of money can buy – its purchasing power (textbook 2.1.4).
Answer: A.
tips: Value of money moves opposite to the price level: inflation lowers purchasing power.

similar_questions.stem: When the general price level doubles, the value of money
explanation_steps: Purchasing power halves. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A 650 Nakfa price tag on a pair of shoes is an example of money functioning as a
explanation_steps: A price tag measures and expresses value in money – the unit of account (measure of value) function. No exchange has happened yet.
Answer: D.
tips: Price labels, accounts and comparisons of value = unit of account.

similar_questions.stem: Using money to pay for a taxi ride illustrates money as a
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: A financial institution which is responsible for issuing bank notes and currency is the
explanation_steps: Textbook: functions of a central (national) bank include ‘Issue bank notes or currency’. In Eritrea this is the Bank of Eritrea.
Answer: A.
tips: Central bank: issues currency, banker to government, lender of last resort, controls money supply.

similar_questions.stem: Which institution is the ‘banker to the government’?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: If the coefficient of the price elasticity of demand is 5.0, then a 10 percent increase in price will result in a ____ percent decrease in the quantity demanded.
explanation_steps: Ped = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP → %ΔQd = Ped × %ΔP = 5.0 × 10 % = 50 %.
Answer: D.
tips: %ΔQ = elasticity × %ΔP.

similar_questions.stem: Ped = 2. Price rises by 8 %. Quantity demanded falls by
explanation_steps: 2 × 8 = 16 %. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes the function of the Commercial Bank of Eritrea?

options.C: Acts as a lender of last resort for depository institution
options.E: Acts as a banker to the government

explanation_steps: The primary functions of commercial banks are accepting deposits and granting loans (textbook).
A, C, D and E are central-bank (Bank of Eritrea) functions. Answer: B.
tips: Commercial bank = deposits + loans; central bank = the bank of banks and of the government.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a primary function of a commercial bank?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: A leftward shift in the supply curve indicates

options.A: that more suppliers have entered the industry.
options.B: decrease in the quantity supplied at each price.
options.C: that more is demanded at each price.
options.D: an increase in the quantity supplied at each price.
options.E: that an increase in income results in an increase in the quantity demanded at each price.

explanation_steps: A leftward (upward) shift of supply = a decrease in supply: less is offered at every price.
More suppliers (A) and D shift it right; C and E are about demand. Answer: B.
tips: Supply shifts left = decrease in supply; a movement along the curve is a change in quantity supplied caused only by the good’s own price.

similar_questions.stem: A drought destroys part of the sorghum crop. The supply curve of sorghum
explanation_steps: Less offered at each price → left. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Change in supply vs quantity supplied

questions.stem: The income elasticity of demand for a bicycle is +10, which implies that a bicycle is
explanation_steps: Positive income elasticity → demand rises with income → normal good (negative = inferior).
The textbook uses exactly this example: “As the income elasticity for bicycles is greater than one, it is considered as a normal good.” Substitute/complement need CROSS elasticity. Answer: C.
tips: Income elasticity: > 0 normal (> 1 luxury), < 0 inferior. Cross elasticity: > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements.

similar_questions.stem: The income elasticity of demand for a good is −0.5. The good is
explanation_steps: Negative → inferior. Answer: B.

questions.stem: To maximise its revenue, a firm

options.A: facing an inelastic demand should always raise its price.
options.B: facing an inelastic demand should always lower its price.
options.C: facing an elastic demand should always raise its price.
options.D: should always charge the highest price possible regardless of the elasticity of demand.
options.E: facing a unitary elasticity should always raise its price.

explanation_steps: Textbook: “An increase in price results in an increase in the total revenue only if the demand … is inelastic. If the demand is elastic, an increase in price will lead to a decrease in the total revenue.”
With unitary elasticity, TR does not change. Answer: A.
tips: Inelastic → raise price to raise TR; elastic → lower price to raise TR.

similar_questions.stem: Demand for a product is elastic. To increase total revenue the seller should
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: ‘always’ is strong (true only while demand stays inelastic), but A is the textbook rule; the other options are clearly wrong.

questions.stem: Question 16 is based on Figure 2 (demand curves DD and D₁D₁; B and C are points on DD, C at a lower price and larger quantity than B; D₁D₁ lies to the right of DD). Which one of the following options <u>is correct</u>?
questions.image_alt: Figure 2. Demand curve: price P on the vertical axis, quantity Q on the horizontal axis. Downward-sloping curve DD with point B (higher price) and point C (lower price, larger quantity) on it; a second curve D₁D₁ lies parallel to the right of DD.

options.A: A movement from point B to point C indicates an increase in demand.
options.B: A shift of curve DD to D₁D₁ indicates a decrease in demand.
options.C: An increase in the quantity demanded is indicated by the movement from point B to point C.
options.D: A change in a supply factor will shift the demand curve DD.
options.E: A movement from point B to point C indicates an increase in supply.

explanation_steps: B → C is a movement ALONG the same demand curve caused by a fall in price: an increase in quantity demanded (not in demand, so A is wrong).
DD → D₁D₁ (to the right) is an increase in demand, so B is wrong; supply factors do not shift demand (D); E confuses demand with supply. Answer: C.
tips: Movement along the curve = change in quantity demanded; shift of the curve = change in demand.

similar_questions.stem: The price of injera falls and people buy more. On a graph this is

options.A: a shift of demand to the right
options.B: a movement down along the demand curve
options.C: a shift of supply to the left
options.D: a shift of demand to the left

explanation_steps: Own-price change → movement along. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Change in quantity demanded versus change in demand

questions.stem: Which of the following is likely to occur if a market <u>is not</u> in equilibrium?

options.A: The demand curve will shift to bring the market to equilibrium.
options.B: The supply curve will shift to bring the market to equilibrium.
options.C: The price will adjust to bring the market to equilibrium.

explanation_steps: A surplus pushes the price down and a shortage pushes it up until Qd = Qs.
The curves do not shift – the price moves along them. Answer: C.
tips: Disequilibrium is corrected by price changes (movements along the curves), not by curve shifts.

similar_questions.stem: At the current price there is a shortage. What will happen?
explanation_steps: Shortage → price rises. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Haile produces 100 units of pens with an average total cost of 50 cents per pen and an average variable cost of 40 cents per pen. What is his total fixed cost in Nakfa?
explanation_steps: AFC = ATC − AVC = 50 − 40 = 10 cents = Nakfa 0.10 per pen.
TFC = AFC × Q = 0.10 × 100 = Nakfa 10.
B (0.10) is the AFC, not the TFC. Answer: D.
tips: ATC = AFC + AVC; multiply an average by quantity to get the total.

questions.stem: Ranking the market structures from most competitive to least competitive, we have

options.A: monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition.
options.B: monopolistic competition, perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly.
options.C: perfect competition, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, monopoly.
options.D: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
options.E: monopolistic competition, perfect competition, oligopoly, monopoly.

explanation_steps: The number of firms falls from many identical firms (perfect competition) → many firms with differentiated products (monopolistic competition) → few firms (oligopoly) → one firm (monopoly).
Answer: D.
tips: Many → many (differentiated) → few → one.

similar_questions.stem: Which market structure has a few large firms?
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: If a firm produces nothing, which of the following costs will be zero?
explanation_steps: Variable costs change with output and are zero at zero output.
Fixed costs (rent, machinery) remain, so total cost = TFC > 0. Answer: A.
tips: At Q = 0: TVC = 0 and TC = TFC.

similar_questions.stem: At zero output, total cost equals
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: The amount of total cost that rises when the firm produces one additional unit is called
explanation_steps: Marginal cost = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ – the extra cost of one more unit.
Answer: E.
tips: Marginal = additional (one more unit).

similar_questions.stem: TC rises from 500 to 540 when output rises from 10 to 11 units. MC =

questions.stem: For perfect competition to exist, there must be

options.B: restriction to the entry of new firms.
options.E: a single seller in the market.

explanation_steps: Perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect information.
A describes oligopoly, E monopoly, B and C are the opposite of the conditions. Answer: D.
tips: Perfect competition = many firms, identical products, free entry, price takers.

similar_questions.stem: In perfect competition products are
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a monopoly is <u>not</u> correct?

options.A: A monopoly is the only seller of the good.
options.B: The good produced by the monopolist has no close substitute.
options.C: Barriers to entry and exist are not present in a monopoly.
options.D: A monopolist does not have any control over the selling price of its good.

explanation_steps: A and B are true. C is false – monopolies exist BECAUSE of strong barriers to entry (‘exist’ is a misprint for ‘exit’).
D is also false – a monopolist is a price maker (textbook: ‘A monopolist has the power to set price’).
So two options (C and D) are ‘not correct’. Both are accepted; C is keyed.
tips: Monopoly: one seller, no close substitutes, high barriers to entry, price maker.

similar_questions.stem: Which is TRUE of a monopolist?

options.C: it is protected by barriers to entry
options.D: its product has many close substitutes

explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Teacher decision: two options are incorrect statements about monopoly – C (no barriers to entry; ‘exist’ misprint for ‘exit’) and D (no control over price). Both accepted; C keyed.

questions.stem: The table shows a hypothetical total utility schedule for a consumer of banana (Table 1: units 0–7 → total utility 0, 90, 190, 270, 350, 420, 420, 400). The consumer begins to experience diminishing marginal utility when she consumes the
explanation_steps: MU = change in TU: 1st 90, 2nd 100, 3rd 80, 4th 80, 5th 70, 6th 0, 7th −20.
MU rises up to the 2nd unit and first falls at the 3rd unit (100 → 80). Answer: A.
tips: Compute MU for every unit first; ‘diminishing’ starts where MU first falls, not where TU falls (7th unit = negative MU).

similar_questions.stem: TU: 1 unit 50, 2 units 110, 3 units 150, 4 units 170. Diminishing MU begins with the
explanation_steps: MU 50, 60, 40, 20 → falls at 3rd. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1 (units 0–7 → total utility 0, 90, 190, 270, 350, 420, 420, 400), you can conclude that the

options.A: marginal utility of the fourth unit of banana is 60 utils.
options.B: marginal utility of the second unit of banana is 270 utils.
options.C: average utility of 3 units of banana is 90 utils.
options.D: average utility of 5 units of banana is 80 utils.
options.E: total utility of 7 units of banana is 1020 utils.

explanation_steps: MU(4) = 350 − 270 = 80 (not 60); MU(2) = 100 (not 270); AU(5) = 420 ÷ 5 = 84 (not 80); TU(7) = 400 (1020 wrongly adds the column). Answer: C.
tips: AU = TU ÷ Q; MU = ΔTU.

similar_questions.stem: TU of 4 units = 200 utils and of 5 units = 230 utils. Which is true?

questions.stem: Indifference curves

options.C: bow outward from the origin of the graph.

explanation_steps: To keep satisfaction constant, more of one good must be offset by less of the other → downward (negative) slope.
They are convex (bowed IN toward the origin) and never cross. Answer: B.
tips: Indifference curves: negative slope, convex to the origin, never intersect, higher = more satisfaction.

similar_questions.stem: Two indifference curves of the same consumer
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: In the circular flow of income and expenditure,

options.A: households sell their factors of production to firms in the factor market.
options.B: households combine factors of production and produce goods and services.
options.C: goods and services offered for sale on the goods market are purchased by firms.
options.D: firms sell factors of production on the goods market.
options.E: households sell goods and services in the factor market.

explanation_steps: Households own the factors (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship) and sell them to firms in the factor market for rent, wages, interest and profit.
Firms combine factors and sell goods to households in the goods market. Answer: A.
tips: Factor market: households → firms (factors). Goods market: firms → households (products).

similar_questions.stem: Wages flow from
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 Circular flow of income and expenditure

questions.stem: The three important injections into the circular flow of income and expenditure are

options.A: investment spending, government expenditure and imports.

explanation_steps: Injections add spending from outside the household–firm loop: investment (I), government expenditure (G) and exports (X).
Leakages (withdrawals) are saving, taxes and imports. Answer: C.
tips: Injections I, G, X ↔ leakages S, T, M.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a leakage from the circular flow?
explanation_steps: Answer: D.

questions.stem: When the Gross Domestic Product is calculated, the

options.A: total value of final services is subtracted from the value of final goods.
options.B: total value of intermediate goods and services is measured in a given period.
options.C: sum of the values added at each stage of production is lower than the spending on final goods and services.
options.D: total value of all final goods and services produced locally is measured in a given period.

explanation_steps: Textbook: GDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced in one year by factors of production located within the territory of a country.
Intermediate goods are excluded (B); total value added EQUALS spending on final goods (C). Answer: D.
tips: GDP = final goods and services, produced within the country, in one period.

similar_questions.stem: Which is excluded from GDP?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: A tax is progressive if

options.A: the tax rate increases with the increase in income.
options.B: it takes a greater percentage of the taxable income of lower income groups than of higher income groups.
options.C: the tax rate decreases with the increase in income.
options.D: the tax rate remains the same for all income levels.
options.E: people with high income pay a small percentage of their incomes.

explanation_steps: Textbook: progressive taxes are ‘taxes whose rates increase with the increase in income’. Eritrea’s income tax (2 % → 30 %) is progressive.
B, C, E describe a regressive tax; D a proportional tax. Answer: A.
tips: Progressive ↑ rate with income; proportional = same rate; regressive ↓ rate with income.

similar_questions.stem: A tax that takes 10 % of every income level is
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: Osman's disposable income increases from 2000 Nakfa to 2500 Nakfa. As a result his saving increases from 300 Nakfa to 450 Nakfa. This implies that his marginal propensity to consume is
explanation_steps: (Check: consumption rises from 1,700 to 2,050, ΔC = 350; 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70.) A (0.30) is the MPS. Answer: B.
tips: MPC = ΔC/ΔYd = 1 − MPS.

similar_questions.stem: Yd rises from 2,500 to 3,000 and saving from 100 to 200. MPC =
explanation_steps: MPS = 100/500 = 0.2 → MPC 0.8. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following increases investment demand?

options.C: An increase in the rate of return on investment
options.D: An increase in the cost of capital goods
options.E: A decrease in the level of profits

explanation_steps: Firms invest when the expected rate of return exceeds the cost of borrowing.
A higher expected return raises investment; higher interest rates (A), costlier capital goods (D) and lower profits (E) reduce it. Answer: C.
tips: Investment is inversely related to the interest rate and directly related to expected returns/profits.

similar_questions.stem: A fall in the interest rate will usually
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Investment – expected rate of return vs interest rate

questions.stem: If the consumption function is given as C = 100 + 3/4Yd, the saving function would be
explanation_steps: Textbook: if C = a + bYd then S = −a + (1 − b)Yd. Answer: B.
tips: Saving intercept = −(consumption intercept); MPS = 1 − MPC.

similar_questions.stem: C = 50 + 0.6Yd. The saving function is
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a public good?
explanation_steps: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable – lighthouses, national defence and traffic lights benefit everyone and nobody can be excluded.
A refrigerator is used only by its buyer (rival, excludable) – a private good. Answer: D.
tips: Public good test: can non-payers be excluded? Does one person’s use reduce another’s?

similar_questions.stem: Which is a public good?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a component of investment?
explanation_steps: Investment (gross domestic investment) includes purchases of new capital goods (machinery), new construction (buildings, bridges – public investment) and changes in inventories.
This is textbook review question 1, p.21. Answer: E.
tips: Investment = new capital goods + construction + change in inventories (not buying shares or second-hand goods).

similar_questions.stem: Which is NOT investment in national income accounting?
explanation_steps: Buying shares is a financial transfer. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a good tax system:
explanation_steps: Textbook characteristics of a good tax system: equity, certainty, convenience, economy/administrative simplicity (low compliance and administration costs), flexibility, productivity.
Answer: E.
tips: Canons of taxation: equity, certainty, convenience, economy.

similar_questions.stem: The principle that the taxpayer should know exactly when and how much to pay is
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Characteristics of a good tax system

questions.stem: In order for a nation to gain from international trade, it must

options.A: have a surplus of a particular product.
options.B: have a comparative advantage in the production of a particular product.
options.C: have an absolute advantage in the production of a particular product.
options.D: have a shortage of one of the factors of production.

explanation_steps: By the theory of comparative advantage, a country gains from trade by specialising in the good it produces at a lower opportunity cost, even if it has no absolute advantage.
Answer: B.
tips: Trade depends on COMPARATIVE (lower opportunity cost), not absolute, advantage.

similar_questions.stem: Country X is better than Y at producing everything. Can both gain from trade?

options.B: Yes, if each specialises according to comparative advantage

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: A country’s transaction with the rest of the world is recorded in its
explanation_steps: Textbook: “A nation’s balance of payments is a summary statement of a country’s transactions with the rest of the world.”
The current, capital and official reserve accounts are only PARTS of it. Answer: C.
tips: BOP = current account + capital account + official reserve account.

similar_questions.stem: Exports and imports of goods are recorded in the

1.3 Is there shortage or surplus of orange juice at a price of 8 Nakfa per glass? (1 point)
questions.answer:
1.1 Diagram: price (Nakfa per glass) on the vertical axis, quantity (glasses per month) on the horizontal axis; a downward-sloping demand curve D through (420, 10) and (300, 15); an upward-sloping supply curve S through (420, 10) and (450, 15); equilibrium E at P = 10, Q = 420; at P = 15 a horizontal line showing Qd = 300 and Qs = 450 with the gap labelled ‘surplus = 150’.
1.2 Surplus: at 15 Nakfa, Qs (450) > Qd (300) → surplus of 150 glasses per month.
1.3 Shortage: 8 Nakfa is below the equilibrium price of 10, so Qd > Qs (demand rises above 420 and supply falls below 420) → shortage.

subparts.question: Draw the demand and supply diagram, properly labelled.
subparts.answer: Axes P (Nakfa/glass) and Q (glasses/month); D through (420, 10) and (300, 15); S through (420, 10) and (450, 15); equilibrium E (420, 10); surplus of 150 marked at P = 15.
steps: Plot the two given points of each curve; they cross at E (420, 10).
Draw a horizontal line at 15 and mark Qd = 300 and Qs = 450.

subparts.question: Shortage or surplus at 8 Nakfa?
subparts.answer: Shortage (Qd > Qs because 8 is below the equilibrium price of 10).

explanation_steps: Equilibrium: Qd = Qs = 420 at P = 10.
At P = 15 (above equilibrium): Qs − Qd = 450 − 300 = 150 → surplus (excess supply). Sellers will cut the price.
At P = 8 (below equilibrium): buyers want more than 420 and sellers offer less than 420 → shortage (excess demand). The price will rise.
Diagram marks: labelled axes (1), correctly sloped and labelled D and S curves through the given points (1), equilibrium point and the surplus at 15 shown (1).
marking_points: 1.1 (3): labelled axes; D downward and S upward through the given points; equilibrium at (420, 10) and surplus at 15 shown.
tips: Above the equilibrium price → surplus; below → shortage. You do not need the exact shortage at 8 – only the direction.

questions.stem:
What are the two accounts in the balance of payments? (2 points)
2.1 ______
2.2 ______
questions.answer:
2.1 Current account (exports and imports of goods and services, income and transfers).
2.2 Capital account (purchases and sales of real and financial assets, borrowing and lending).
explanation_steps: The textbook lists three main accounts: the current account, the capital account and the official reserve account.
The official reserve account only balances the other two (current + capital + reserves = 0), so the two main accounts asked for are the current account and the capital account.
marking_points: 1 point each: current account; capital account. (Official reserve account can be accepted as an extra, but the question asks for two.)
tips: Current = trade in goods and services (+ income, transfers); capital = flows of assets and loans.

similar_questions.answer: Capital account (purchase of real assets abroad).
explanation_steps: Asset purchases and investment flows → capital account.

questions.stem:
What are the three approaches (methods) of calculating GDP? (3 points)
3.1 ______
3.2 ______
3.3 ______
questions.answer:
3.1 Expenditure approach (GDP = C + I + G + NX).
3.2 Income approach (sum of factor incomes: wages, rent, interest, profit).
3.3 Value-added (output/product) approach (sum of the values added by all producers or sectors – agriculture, industry, services).
explanation_steps: Textbook: ‘There are three methods of measuring a country’s GNP or GDP: (i) Expenditure method … (ii) Income method … (iii) Value added approach.’
All three give the same total because every Nakfa spent on final output becomes someone’s income, and the sum of values added equals the value of final goods.
marking_points: 1 point each: expenditure; income; value added (output/product) approach.
tips: Remember E-I-V: Expenditure, Income, Value added.

similar_questions.stem: Which GDP method adds consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports?
explanation_steps: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).

questions.stem:
Massawa Fish Processing Plant is a private enterprise employing one general manager, two fish processing employees, and two sales personnel. All employees are subject to income tax deduction. The following information pertains to their wages and salaries for the month of January 2018. All amounts are in Nakfa. (5 points)
Rahwa (Manager) basic 15,000, gross 15,000; Ali (Sales) basic 7,000 + commission 2,000 = 9,000; Berhane (Sales) basic 5,500 + commission 1,500 = 7,000; Suleiman (Fish processing) basic 5,000 + overtime 3,000 = 8,000; Meriem (Fish processing) basic 3,500 + overtime 2,000 = 5,500.
Tax table: 1–200: 2 %; 201–1,200: 10 %; 1,201–2,500: 20 %; 2,501–3,500: 25 %; over 3,500: 30 %.
Required: Using the information above, compute their respective net pay in Nakfa. 5.1 Rahwa 5.2 Ali 5.3 Berhane 5.4 Suleiman 5.5 Meriem

answer_tables.title: Net pay computation (Tax = Gross × 30 % − 436 for gross over 3,500)

explanation_steps: All gross salaries are over 3,500, so each person’s tax = Gross × 30 % − 436. (436 = the tax saved because the first 3,500 is taxed at lower rates: 3,500 × 30 % − (4 + 100 + 260 + 250) = 1,050 − 614.)
tips: Use Gross × rate − constant (436 for the 30 % bracket) – much faster than bracket-by-bracket, and the result is identical.
Overtime and commission are part of gross pay and are taxed too.
